concepts.title: Authentication, Authorization, and the Security Filter Chain
concepts.description: Authentication answers the question 'who are you,' authorization answers the separate question 'what are you allowed to do,' and Spring Security enforces both by running every request through a chain of servlet filters that sits in front of your controllers, not inside them.
learningObjectives: Distinguish authentication from authorization with a concrete example of each one failing independently of the other.
Explain, conceptually, what the Spring Security filter chain is and where it sits relative to DispatcherServlet.
Explain the role of the SecurityContext and SecurityContextHolder in carrying the authenticated principal through a request.
Explain which HTTP status results from an authentication failure versus an authorization failure, and why they differ.
Predict how simply adding spring-boot-starter-security to a project changes an application's behavior with zero configuration written.

sections.heading: Two Different Questions: Who Are You, and What Can You Do
sections.body:
**Authentication** answers 'who are you?': it verifies that a set of presented credentials (a username and password, a bearer token, a client certificate) corresponds to a real identity. **Authorization** answers a separate question: 'given that you are who you say you are, are you allowed to do *this specific thing*?' The two checks are independent, and mixing them up is a common source of confused bug reports. A request can fail authentication (the server has no idea who this is) or pass authentication and still fail authorization (the server knows exactly who this is, and that identity isn't permitted to perform this action).

A request with no credentials, or credentials that match no known identity, fails authentication, and the client learns it must (re-)authenticate. A request from a legitimate, authenticated user, say a regular customer, hitting an admin-only endpoint like `DELETE /api/admin/users/7` fails authorization instead: the server knows who is asking, and the answer is 'a real user, but not one permitted to do this.' Getting a login form to work (authentication) and getting role-based access control right (authorization) are separate engineering problems, even though one framework, Spring Security, handles both.

sections.heading: The Filter Chain: Security Runs Before Your Code Ever Sees the Request
sections.body:
Spring Security is implemented as a chain of servlet `Filter`s, registered at the servlet-container level *in front of* `DispatcherServlet`. Security decisions are therefore made before Spring MVC's routing and handler mapping (covered in the Building REST APIs module) run at all, and a rejected request is turned away before your controller code has any chance to execute. That is the point: security that only kicks in once you're inside a controller method is easy to skip by accident on some new endpoint you forget to guard.

A simplified request passes through filters with these responsibilities, in order. First, something extracts and parses credentials from the request (a filter reading an `Authorization: Basic ...` header, or a form-login filter reading posted username and password fields) and attempts to authenticate them. Next, an authorization-decision filter checks whether the resulting authentication, or the lack of one, is permitted to access the requested URL and HTTP method. Finally, an exception-translation filter catches security failures thrown by the earlier filters and converts them into the right HTTP response (`401` or `403`, covered next) instead of letting them surface as a generic error. Each filter decides whether to hand the request to the next one or stop it there, and only a request that survives every filter reaches `DispatcherServlet` and, eventually, your controller.

sections.heading: SecurityContextHolder and the Authenticated Principal
sections.body:
Once a request is authenticated, Spring Security has to make that fact available to the rest of the request's processing (your controller, your service layer, the method-security checks covered in the next concept) without re-authenticating at every step. It does this with an `Authentication` object: a container holding the identified principal (typically a `UserDetails` implementation, or just a username), the credentials used (usually cleared once authentication succeeds), and a list of `GrantedAuthority` objects describing what the principal may do (roles like `ROLE_ADMIN`, or finer-grained permissions).

That `Authentication` is stored in a `SecurityContext`, held by `SecurityContextHolder`. By default the holder is backed by a `ThreadLocal`, so the context is scoped to the single thread handling this request. It is populated near the start of the filter chain and available anywhere downstream on that thread: in your controller (through an `Authentication` or `Principal` method parameter that Spring MVC resolves for you) or in your service layer (through `SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication()`). It is cleared at the end of the request so that one request's identity can never leak into another's, which matters on a server that reuses a shared thread pool for many concurrent requests. The flip side is that a thread you start yourself, or an `@Async` method, does not see the request's identity by default. Spring Security provides wrappers such as `DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor` that copy the context to the new thread, so code that hands work to another thread has to opt in.

sections.heading: What Adding spring-boot-starter-security Changes By Default
sections.body:
Consistent with the autoconfiguration approach from the Core Concepts module, adding `spring-boot-starter-security` as a dependency, with no security code written, changes your application's behavior immediately, because Spring Boot's security autoconfiguration activates as soon as the relevant classes are on the classpath. **Every endpoint becomes secured by default** and requires authentication. A default in-memory user named `user` is created with a randomly generated password, printed once in the startup logs (a line like `Using generated security password: 8e557245-...`). An unauthenticated request is rejected with `401 Unauthorized`, and a browser request is redirected to a default login form. For a non-browser client using HTTP Basic, the 401 response carries a `WWW-Authenticate: Basic` header telling the client how to authenticate.

The all-or-nothing lockdown is a fail-safe choice: Spring Boot would rather you notice immediately that adding security changed everything than ship an application with sensitive endpoints open because no security configuration existed yet. It is still a common source of confusion the first time a team adds the starter, because endpoints that were intentionally public suddenly return `401` with no security configuration class in sight to explain why. The fix is a deliberate `SecurityFilterChain` bean that declares which endpoints are public and which require authentication or a specific role, which is the subject of the next concept.

examples.title: Two Requests, Two Different Failure Modes
examples.code:
# Request 1: no credentials supplied at all
GET /api/admin/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

# Response: 401 Unauthorized
# Spring Security has no idea who is making this request.


# Request 2: valid credentials for a real, authenticated user -- but that
# user only has ROLE_CUSTOMER, and this endpoint requires ROLE_ADMIN
GET /api/admin/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Basic YW15OnBhc3N3b3JkMTIz

# Response: 403 Forbidden
# Spring Security knows who this is; that identity is not
# permitted to access this resource.
examples.explanation: Both requests are rejected, but for different reasons that map to different HTTP statuses. The first fails authentication: there is no Authorization header, so the server cannot establish an identity, and 401 Unauthorized is the standard response for 'you have not proven who you are.' The second passes authentication (the credentials are valid and belong to a known user) but fails authorization: the user's granted authorities don't include what this endpoint's access rule requires, and 403 Forbidden is the standard response for 'you are known, but you are not allowed to do this.' Collapsing both into one generic error would hide useful diagnostic information from developers and, within reason, from legitimate API consumers.

examples.title: The Filter Chain, Conceptually, Ahead of DispatcherServlet
examples.explanation: This is a simplified ordering of responsibilities, not an exhaustive or exact list of Spring Security's internal filter classes, but the structure is accurate: authentication filters run, then an authorization decision is made, then any security exception from either stage is translated into the right HTTP status, and all of it happens before DispatcherServlet, the class that routes to your controllers, is invoked. A request turned away at step 2 or 3 never reaches step 5, so the controller method's body never runs. That is why an if-check inside a controller method is both redundant with, and weaker than, enforcement at this earlier layer.

examples.title: Reading the Authenticated Principal Inside a Controller
examples.explanation: Spring MVC resolves Authentication and Principal as special argument types for a controller method, with no @RequestParam-style annotation: it takes the current Authentication from SecurityContextHolder (the SecurityContext for this request's thread) and hands it in. By the time this method runs, the filter chain has already established who the request belongs to, so the controller doesn't authenticate anything itself, it reads the identity the chain already determined. That is the practical payoff of SecurityContextHolder: any code later in the same request's thread, whether controller or service, can ask 'who is this?' without re-running authentication logic.

misconceptions.description: Authentication and authorization are the same concept: two words people use interchangeably for 'security.'
misconceptions.clarification: They answer different questions and fail independently. Authentication establishes identity: who is making this request, verified via credentials. Authorization is a separate decision made AFTER identity is established: is this now-known identity permitted to perform this action or access this resource. A fully authenticated, legitimate user can still be correctly denied access to an admin-only endpoint (authorization failure, 403), while a request with no credentials never reaches an authorization decision, because there is no identity yet to evaluate (authentication failure, 401).

misconceptions.description: Spring Security only takes effect once a request reaches your controller method, so an if-check inside the method body is a reliable way to fully secure an endpoint.
misconceptions.clarification: Spring Security is implemented as a chain of servlet filters that runs at the servlet-container level, strictly BEFORE DispatcherServlet and therefore before ANY controller method gets a chance to execute. A request that fails authentication or authorization is turned away by the filter chain itself, and the controller method's body never runs, so there is nothing for an if-check inside it to guard against for that failure. Relying on manual in-method checks as the primary mechanism is weaker than configuring the filter chain correctly (the subject of the next concept): it is easy to forget the check on a new endpoint, whereas a centralized filter-chain rule applies automatically to every matching request, with no per-method code.
misconceptions.fact: Spring Security is implemented as a chain of servlet filters that runs at the servlet-container level, strictly BEFORE DispatcherServlet and therefore before any controller method can execute.

exercises.prompt:
A REST API has an endpoint GET /api/admin/audit-log that requires the caller to be authenticated AND to hold ROLE_ADMIN. Predict the HTTP status for each of these two requests, and explain why they differ.

Request A: sent with no Authorization header at all.
Request B: sent with a valid Authorization header for a real, successfully-authenticated user who only holds ROLE_CUSTOMER.
exercises.code:
// Request A
GET /api/admin/audit-log HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

// Request B
GET /api/admin/audit-log HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Basic <valid credentials for a ROLE_CUSTOMER user>
hints: For Request A, can the server establish any identity at all from what was sent? If not, which of the two security questions (authn or authz) never even gets a chance to be asked?
For Request B, the server CAN establish a real identity -- so does it fail at the 'who are you' stage, or at the 'what are you allowed to do' stage?
401 corresponds to one of these two questions failing; 403 corresponds to the other. Match each request to the specific question it fails.
exercises.expectedAnswer: Request A returns 401 Unauthorized, because no credentials were supplied at all -- the server cannot establish any identity, so authentication itself fails before an authorization decision is even possible. Request B returns 403 Forbidden, because the credentials ARE valid and correspond to a real, known user (authentication succeeds), but that user's granted authorities (ROLE_CUSTOMER) don't satisfy this endpoint's requirement of ROLE_ADMIN, so the request is correctly denied at the authorization stage instead.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The two requests fail at different, sequential stages of the filter chain. Request A has no credential to authenticate, so the authentication stage fails, and Spring Security's exception-translation filter converts that into 401 Unauthorized, the standard response for 'you have not established who you are.' Request B's credentials are valid, so authentication succeeds and an Authentication object with ROLE_CUSTOMER among its granted authorities is placed into the SecurityContext. The authorization stage then checks that authority list against this endpoint's requirement (ROLE_ADMIN), finds no match, and denies the request with 403 Forbidden, the standard response for 'you are known, but not permitted to do this.' The distinction matters in practice: a client that gets 401 knows it needs to (re-)authenticate, while a client that gets 403 knows that authenticating again as the same user won't help.

exercises.prompt: A team adds spring-boot-starter-security to their project's build file to prepare for adding real login functionality later. After restarting the application, every single endpoint -- including ones that were always meant to be public, like GET /api/health -- now returns 401 Unauthorized, and no security configuration class exists anywhere in the codebase yet. Explain what's actually happening, and describe, at a high level, the shape of the fix (full implementation is covered in the next concept).
hints: This isn't a bug in the traditional sense -- nothing is broken. What does Spring Boot's security autoconfiguration do by default the moment the starter is present on the classpath, with zero configuration written?
The generated password log line is a strong clue about what default behavior just activated -- a default in-memory user was created, and every endpoint now requires SOME authenticated identity.

The actual fix isn't about removing the starter -- it's about writing an explicit SecurityFilterChain bean that declares GET /api/health (and any other genuinely public endpoints) as permitAll(), while requiring authentication for the rest. That's the subject of the next concept.
exercises.solutionExplanation: This is Spring Boot's intended, fail-safe default. As soon as spring-boot-starter-security is on the classpath, its autoconfiguration locks down EVERY endpoint behind authentication, creates a single in-memory user named 'user' with a random password (printed once in the startup logs so you can log in and confirm security is active), and rejects any unauthenticated request with 401. Spring Boot would rather an application become loudly inaccessible when security is added than let a team assume 'we added the dependency, so we must be secure now' while some endpoint stays silently open. Nothing is broken; the team just hasn't yet written the configuration that declares which endpoints, like /api/health, are public. The fix is a SecurityFilterChain bean, built with HttpSecurity, that marks specific paths as permitAll() and requires authentication for the rest, replacing the blanket default with a deliberate, reviewable policy. That is the subject of the next concept.

assessments.prompt: A request to a protected endpoint includes valid, correctly-verified credentials for a real user account, but that user's role does not permit the specific action being requested. What HTTP status should the server return, and why?
options: 401 Unauthorized, because the user is still not permitted to complete the request, which is what 'unauthorized' means.
200 OK with an error message in the response body, since the request itself was well-formed and reached a real endpoint.
500 Internal Server Error, because a mismatch between a user's role and the requested action indicates a server-side configuration bug, so it should be reported as a server fault to be fixed.
403 Forbidden, because authentication succeeded (the identity is genuinely known and verified) but authorization failed -- the known identity simply isn't permitted to perform this action.
assessments.explanation: Authentication and authorization are distinct checks that can succeed or fail independently. Here authentication succeeds, since the credentials are valid and belong to a known identity, so a 401, which signals a failure to establish identity, would be misleading despite 'unauthorized' appearing in its name. The failure is at the authorization stage: the known identity's authorities don't satisfy what the action requires, which is the case 403 Forbidden exists for. The “500 Internal Server Error, because a mismatch…” option is wrong because this is an expected, correctly functioning access-control outcome, not a bug. The “200 OK with an error message…” option is wrong because returning 200 for a denied request would hide the access-control decision from the client and from any tooling that inspects status codes.

assessments.prompt: A request fails Spring Security's authentication filter -- no valid credentials were supplied. What happens to that request afterward?
options: DispatcherServlet routes it to a special @ExceptionHandler-annotated controller method reserved specifically for security failures.

It never reaches DispatcherServlet at all -- an exception-translation filter converts the authentication failure into a 401 response directly within the filter chain, before Spring MVC's own routing and handler mapping ever run.

It's forwarded to DispatcherServlet anyway, and the controller method is expected to inspect the Authentication object itself and reject invalid requests from inside the method body, because the filter chain only records the failure.
It's queued and automatically retried by the filter chain up to a fixed number of times before finally being rejected.
assessments.explanation: Spring Security's filter chain is registered in front of DispatcherServlet so that a rejected request is turned away before any controller code, or DispatcherServlet's routing, runs. An authentication failure is caught and translated into 401 by a filter within that chain, and the request goes no further. The “It's forwarded to DispatcherServlet anyway…” option describes the weak, easy-to-forget pattern this concept warns against: security enforced only through manual in-method checks. The “It's queued and automatically retried…” and “DispatcherServlet routes it to a special @ExceptionHandler-annotated…” options invent retry and exception-handler dispatch mechanisms the filter chain does not have.

assessments.prompt: SecurityContextHolder is, by default, backed by a ThreadLocal. What is the practical consequence of this design choice?
options: Every new thread the application spawns automatically inherits the current request's SecurityContext with no extra configuration required.
The authenticated identity is shared globally across every request the application is handling concurrently, since ThreadLocal values are visible application-wide.

The authenticated identity is scoped to the single thread handling one specific request, populated near the start of the filter chain and cleared at the end of that request -- so one request's identity can never accidentally leak into another's on a shared thread pool.
ThreadLocal storage means the SecurityContext is persisted to disk, surviving an application restart.
assessments.explanation: A ThreadLocal is scoped to one thread, which is why it fits here: the identity resolved early in a request's trip through the filter chain is available to any code later on that thread (controller, service, or otherwise), and it is cleared at the end of the request so it can't bleed into a different request handled by the same pooled thread. The “The authenticated identity is shared globally across…” option describes the opposite of what ThreadLocal provides, which is isolation. The “ThreadLocal storage means the SecurityContext is persisted…” option confuses in-memory, per-thread storage with persistence. The “Every new thread the application spawns automatically…” option is false: a thread you spawn yourself does not inherit another thread's ThreadLocal value.

assessments.prompt: A team adds spring-boot-starter-security to a fresh project with zero security configuration written, then starts the application and checks the startup logs. What do they find, and what does it mean for accessing a now-protected endpoint?
options: A line resembling 'Using generated security password: <uuid>' is printed once in the logs -- Spring Boot created a single in-memory user named 'user' with that randomly generated password, usable to authenticate against any endpoint until real security configuration replaces this default.
No password is generated at all -- the default user account has no password, and any request is accepted automatically without credentials.
The application refuses to start until a SecurityConfig class defining a real user store is provided.
The generated password is written permanently into application.properties, so it stays the same across every future restart.
assessments.explanation: This is the default behavior described in the lesson: adding the starter with no configuration locks down every endpoint, creates one in-memory user named 'user', and prints that user's random password once in the startup log so someone can log in and confirm security is active. The “No password is generated at all…” option is wrong, since a non-empty password is always generated. The “The application refuses to start until…” option is wrong: the application boots fine with this default. The “The generated password is written permanently into…” option is wrong: the password is generated fresh at each startup (unless you override it) and is never written to a properties file.

assessments.prompt: Explain to a developer who has never worked with Spring Security before what the filter chain is, why it runs where it does relative to DispatcherServlet, and how the SecurityContextHolder lets later code know who's making the current request without re-authenticating.
assessments.modelAnswer: Spring Security is built as a sequence of ordinary servlet filters, the mechanism the servlet API provides for code that must run against every incoming request before it reaches the application's handling logic. The chain is registered at the servlet-container level, in front of DispatcherServlet, the single servlet that routes requests to your @RestController methods. That positioning is deliberate: every security decision (who is making the request, and whether that identity may do what it asks) happens BEFORE Spring MVC's routing runs, and therefore before any of your controller code can execute. A rejected request never reaches your business logic, and there is no way to slip past security by calling a controller method directly, because the method is unreachable except through the whole chain. Within the chain, one stage handles authentication: it extracts whatever credentials the request carries (a header, a cookie, posted form fields, depending on configuration), verifies them against known identities, and on success packages the result into an Authentication object holding the identity, its granted authorities (roles or permissions) and, usually cleared, the credentials. That object is stored in a SecurityContext, which SecurityContextHolder makes available for the rest of the request on the same thread. By default it is backed by a ThreadLocal, so it is scoped to the one request being handled and cleared when the request finishes, which keeps one request's identity from leaking into another on a shared thread pool. This is why a controller, or a service further down the call stack, can ask 'who is the current user?' (through an Authentication or Principal parameter, or SecurityContextHolder directly) without doing any authentication itself: that work happened once, earlier in the same request, and the result is waiting to be read.

concepts.title: Securing Endpoints with HttpSecurity and Method Security
concepts.description: HttpSecurity lets you declare, in one place, exactly which URL patterns are public and which require authentication or a specific role, while method-security annotations like @PreAuthorize push that same access-control decision down onto individual service methods -- two complementary tools for two different levels of granularity.
learningObjectives: Configure a SecurityFilterChain bean using HttpSecurity to permit certain paths and require authentication or a specific role for others.
Explain why rule order matters within authorizeHttpRequests and predict which of two overlapping rules wins for a given request.
Use @PreAuthorize for method-level authorization and explain how it differs in granularity from URL-based HttpSecurity rules.
Explain why @EnableMethodSecurity is required for @PreAuthorize to have any effect, and what happens -- silently -- if it's forgotten.
Explain the self-invocation limitation of proxy-based method security as a known edge case.

sections.heading: Declaring URL-Level Rules with HttpSecurity
From WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter to a SecurityFilterChain Bean
sections.body: Older Spring Security tutorials and codebases configure security by extending a base class, `WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter`, and overriding `configure(HttpSecurity http)`. That class was deprecated in Spring Security 5.7 and removed in Spring Security 6 in favor of the `SecurityFilterChain` bean style shown above. Spring Boot generally prefers composition to inheritance-based configuration, and the bean style is more flexible: a class can extend only one base class, but an application can register several independent `SecurityFilterChain` beans, each scoped to a different set of paths with `securityMatcher(...)`, for different security policies in different parts of the same application. It is also consistent with how the rest of Spring Boot expects you to contribute configuration.

sections.heading: Method Security with @PreAuthorize
@EnableMethodSecurity: The Easy-to-Forget Switch

examples.title: A SecurityFilterChain With Correctly Ordered Rules
examples.explanation: Rules are listed from most specific to least specific, which matters because Spring Security evaluates them in order and stops at the first match. /api/public/** is checked first, so anything under that path gets permitAll() before the broader rules can apply. /api/admin/** requires ROLE_ADMIN. GET requests to /api/orders/** are also restricted by HTTP method and allow either CUSTOMER or ADMIN. Last, anyRequest().authenticated() is the catch-all for every path not matched above, requiring a valid authenticated identity with no specific role. @EnableMethodSecurity is present too, which is what makes @PreAuthorize (used in the next example) take effect anywhere in the application.

examples.title: Method Security Enforced Regardless of Caller
examples.explanation: NightlyRefundBatchJob calls issueRefund(...) with no HTTP request or URL involved, so a URL-based HttpSecurity rule restricting /api/refunds/** to ROLE_ADMIN would give no protection here: the call never goes through that URL, or any URL. Because @PreAuthorize is attached to issueRefund itself, the same check runs whatever calls it (an HTTP-triggered controller, this scheduled job, any other bean). That is the case where method security earns its place alongside URL rules, not instead of them. Note that a scheduled job has no authenticated user by default, so this call would be rejected unless the job sets up a security context with an ADMIN principal.

examples.title: Rule Order Bug: A Broad Rule Swallowing a Specific One
examples.explanation: In the broken version, `/api/**` is declared first and matches everything under /api, including /api/public/status. Because Spring Security stops at the first matching rule, no request ever reaches the /api/public/** rule beneath it, so public requests require authentication, and the /api/admin/** rule below it is shadowed too, which means any authenticated user can reach the admin paths. The bug is structural: the later rules aren't wrong, they are unreachable. Swapping the order fixes it with no change to either rule, because the specific rules are then evaluated and matched before the broad one can claim the request.

misconceptions.description: Rules inside authorizeHttpRequests are evaluated as a complete set, and the most specific matching rule always wins automatically, regardless of the order they happen to be written in.
misconceptions.clarification: Spring Security evaluates authorizeHttpRequests rules in the order they're declared and stops at the FIRST rule that matches. There is no automatic 'most specific wins' resolution, unlike CSS specificity or some routing frameworks. A broad pattern (like `/api/**`) declared before a narrower one makes the narrower rule unreachable purely because of ordering, even though that rule is correct in isolation. Order rules from most specific to least specific and finish with a catch-all anyRequest().

misconceptions.description: @PreAuthorize works automatically the moment it's placed on a method, as long as Spring Security itself is on the classpath and configured somewhere in the app.
misconceptions.clarification: @PreAuthorize needs @EnableMethodSecurity on some @Configuration class before it has ANY effect. Without it the annotation is inert metadata that Spring never reads, and the annotated method runs unguarded for every caller. There is no error, warning or startup failure to signal the gap: the application runs, the code compiles and the annotation sits visibly on the method, which is what makes forgetting @EnableMethodSecurity easy to miss. A test that only checks the happy path (an authorized caller succeeding) would never catch it, so also test that an UNauthorized caller is rejected.

exercises.prompt: Requests to GET /api/public/status are unexpectedly returning 401 Unauthorized, even though this SecurityFilterChain clearly includes a permitAll() rule for /api/public/**. Find and fix the ordering bug.
hints: authorizeHttpRequests rules are matched in the order they're declared, and evaluation stops at the FIRST rule that matches. Which requests does the first rule here match?
If a broad rule is declared first, can a rule declared after it be reached for any request that the broad rule already matches?
Reorder the rules so the specific patterns (/api/public/**, /api/admin/**) come before the broader /api/** rule.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `/api/**` matches every path under /api, and because it was declared FIRST, Spring Security's first-match-wins evaluation stops there for those requests, including /api/public/status. The permitAll() and hasRole("ADMIN") rules declared afterward are unreachable for anything under /api, since no such request can fail to match `/api/**` and fall through to them. That is why GET /api/public/status required authentication: it matched `/api/**` before it could reach the intended permitAll() rule. (The admin rule was shadowed too, so any authenticated user could reach /api/admin/** until this was fixed.) Moving the specific rules ahead of the broad one restores the intended behavior: a request to /api/public/** matches the permissive rule first.

exercises.prompt: A ReportService method is annotated @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')"), but a manual test confirms a non-admin user can still call it successfully and get real data back -- the security check appears to be doing nothing at all. Find and fix the bug, given that the SecurityConfig class below is the only security configuration in the application.
hints: @PreAuthorize needs a specific, separate annotation elsewhere in the application before it has any effect at all -- is that annotation present anywhere in SecurityConfig?
Without that annotation, Spring never wraps ReportService in the AOP proxy responsible for actually evaluating @PreAuthorize expressions before a method runs.
Add the missing annotation directly to the SecurityConfig class (or any other @Configuration class) to activate method security application-wide.
exercises.solutionExplanation: @PreAuthorize is inert without @EnableMethodSecurity on some @Configuration class. Spring wraps beans in the AOP proxy that evaluates method-security annotations only when told to, and SecurityConfig never declared it. With no proxy, getAllReports() ran like any ordinary unguarded method for every caller, which is why the non-admin's manual test succeeded. Adding @EnableMethodSecurity to SecurityConfig makes Spring create that proxy around ReportService (and every other bean with method-security annotations), so calls to getAllReports() are intercepted and checked against the current Authentication's authorities before the method body runs, and a caller without ROLE_ADMIN is rejected.

assessments.prompt: A SecurityFilterChain declares, in this exact order: (1) requestMatchers("/api/orders/**").hasRole("CUSTOMER"), (2) requestMatchers("/api/orders/summary").permitAll(), (3) anyRequest().authenticated(). A request arrives for GET /api/orders/summary. Which rule actually governs this request?
options: Rule 3, because anyRequest() is a more general, catch-all rule that Spring Security always evaluates last regardless of declaration order in the configuration.
Rule 1, because it's declared first and its pattern (/api/orders/**) matches /api/orders/summary, and Spring Security stops at the first matching rule.
Rule 2, because permitAll() always takes precedence over role-based rules regardless of where it's declared.
All three rules are combined, and the request is permitted only if it satisfies every one of them simultaneously.
assessments.explanation: Spring Security evaluates authorizeHttpRequests rules in declared order and stops at the first match. Nothing makes permitAll() win regardless of position (so the “Rule 2, because permitAll() always takes precedence…” option is wrong), and anyRequest() isn't deferred to the end unless it is written last (so the “Rule 3, because anyRequest() is a more…” option is wrong, since rule 1 matches first). /api/orders/** matches /api/orders/summary and rule 1 is declared before rule 2, so rule 1 (hasRole("CUSTOMER")) governs the request. Rule 2's permitAll(), though it looks aimed at this exact path, is unreachable because rule 1 already claimed the match. The “All three rules are combined…” option describes AND-combination, which rule evaluation does not do: exactly one rule applies, whichever matches first.

assessments.prompt: An older tutorial configures security by extending WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter and overriding configure(HttpSecurity http). What is true about this approach in a modern (Spring Security 6+) Spring Boot application?
options: WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was deprecated starting with Spring Security 5.7 and removed entirely in Spring Security 6, replaced by declaring a SecurityFilterChain as a @Bean -- partly because a class can only extend one base class, while an application can register several independent SecurityFilterChain beans covering different parts of the same application.
It still works identically -- WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was deprecated purely for cosmetic, naming-convention reasons.
WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter remains required for any application that needs more than one distinct security policy.
The @Bean-based style is only a valid alternative if @EnableWebSecurity is removed from the application entirely.
assessments.explanation: The inheritance-based WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was deprecated in 5.7 and removed in Spring Security 6 in favor of an explicit @Bean returning a SecurityFilterChain, partly because composition (several independent beans, each scoped with securityMatcher(...)) is more flexible than extending one base class. The “It still works identically…” option understates the reason, which is architectural and not cosmetic. The “WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter remains required for any application…” option inverts the situation: the @Bean style is what makes multiple independent policies easy. The “The @Bean-based style is only a valid…” option invents a dependency between the two annotations that doesn't exist.

assessments.prompt: A @Service class has two methods: publicMethod() (no security annotation) and sensitiveMethod() (annotated @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")). publicMethod() calls sensitiveMethod() directly on itself, from within the same class, using `this.sensitiveMethod()`. A non-admin caller invokes publicMethod() from a controller, with @EnableMethodSecurity correctly configured. What happens?
options: Spring automatically rewrites the self-invocation into a proxy-routed call at compile time via annotation processing.

The @PreAuthorize check on sensitiveMethod() is still enforced correctly, rejecting the non-admin caller, because Spring intercepts every method call to an annotated method regardless of where the call originates.
The @PreAuthorize check is bypassed entirely for this particular call.
The application fails to start, because Spring detects this self-invocation pattern at startup and refuses to register the bean.
assessments.explanation: Self-invocation is a known limitation of proxy-based Spring AOP: the proxy wraps the bean from the outside, so only calls that arrive through the proxy (from another bean, or from outside the class) are intercepted. A call on `this` from within the same class bypasses the proxy and therefore the security check, even with @EnableMethodSecurity configured. The “The @PreAuthorize check on sensitiveMethod() is still…” option states the naive assumption this limitation contradicts. The “The application fails to start, because Spring…” and “Spring automatically rewrites the self-invocation into…” options invent protective or rewriting behavior that proxy-based AOP does not have.

assessments.prompt: A team's test suite for ReportService.getAllReports() (annotated @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")) only ever calls the method as an admin user, and every test passes. @EnableMethodSecurity was never added anywhere in the application. What does this passing test suite actually demonstrate?
options: It proves @EnableMethodSecurity must already be present somewhere, since @PreAuthorize could not have compiled without it.
It indicates the test suite simply needs more admin-role test cases before the result can be considered conclusive.
It confirms method security is correctly enforced, since the annotated method behaved as expected for the admin case.

Very little about enforcement -- because the method also runs completely unguarded for ANY caller when @EnableMethodSecurity is missing, a test that only ever exercises the authorized happy path would pass identically whether or not the security check is actually active at all.
assessments.explanation: Without @EnableMethodSecurity, @PreAuthorize does nothing, so an unguarded method and a correctly guarded one behave identically for a caller who is allowed to call it. The admin-only happy-path test passes either way, which is why the lesson recommends testing that an UNauthorized caller is rejected, instead of trusting the annotation's presence or a passing happy-path test. The “It confirms method security is correctly enforced…” option treats a happy-path pass as proof of enforcement. The “It proves @EnableMethodSecurity must already be present…” option is false: @PreAuthorize compiles as valid, inert metadata whether or not @EnableMethodSecurity exists. The “It indicates the test suite simply needs…” option misdiagnoses the gap, which is a missing negative test, not a shortage of positive ones.

assessments.prompt: Explain the difference between securing an operation with a URL-based rule in HttpSecurity versus securing it with @PreAuthorize on the underlying service method, including a concrete scenario where only one of the two would actually provide protection, and explain the @EnableMethodSecurity requirement.
assessments.modelAnswer: A URL-based rule declared with authorizeHttpRequests on a SecurityFilterChain governs access at the entry point into the application. It inspects the HTTP request's path and method and decides, before DispatcherServlet routes the request, whether that URL is reachable for the current (or absent) authentication. That makes it a good, centralized way to lock down an area of the API ('nothing under /api/admin/** is reachable without ROLE_ADMIN') with one rule covering every controller method under that path. But its protection is tied to requests arriving through that URL. It does not protect the same business logic when it is invoked another way: a scheduled job, an internal call from another bean, a message listener, none of which involve an HTTP request. @PreAuthorize on the method that implements the sensitive operation closes that gap, because the check is attached to the operation and not to any route into it, so it is evaluated whatever calls the method. If RefundService.issueRefund(...) is reachable through a REST endpoint AND a nightly batch job, a URL rule on the endpoint alone leaves the job's call unguarded, and only @PreAuthorize on issueRefund protects both paths. That protection doesn't activate by itself: @PreAuthorize is only an annotation until @EnableMethodSecurity is declared on some @Configuration class, which tells Spring to wrap eligible beans in an AOP proxy that evaluates the expression before the real method runs. Forgetting it produces no error or warning, and the method runs unguarded for every caller, so the gap stays silent instead of failing loudly.

concepts.title: Password Hashing with BCrypt
concepts.description: Storing a password requires a slow, automatically-salted, one-way hash like BCrypt rather than plain text or reversible encryption, because an application should never be capable of recovering a user's raw password again -- only of verifying a claimed one.
learningObjectives: Explain why storing passwords in plain text, or with reversible encryption, is wrong even when the database itself is otherwise well protected.
Explain what a one-way hash function is and why irreversibility is the property that actually matters for password storage.
Explain what a salt is, why it defeats precomputed lookup-table attacks, and how BCrypt manages salting automatically.
Explain why BCrypt is deliberately slow via a tunable work factor, and why that slowness is a security feature rather than a performance defect.
Use PasswordEncoder.encode() and matches() correctly, and explain why comparing two independently-produced hashes with plain string equality is not a reliable way to verify a password.

sections.heading: Why Plain Text and Reversible Encryption Are Both Wrong
sections.body:
Storing a password as plain text means anyone who can read the database reads every user's usable password immediately. That could be a direct breach, an exposed backup, an overly broad internal database permission, or a verbose log statement. Because people reuse passwords across unrelated services, a leak from one poorly secured application routinely compromises accounts on other systems too, so the damage is not contained to 'just this one app.'

Reversible *encryption* looks like an improvement, since the stored value isn't the raw password, but it only shifts the problem. Encryption is designed to be decrypted by whoever holds the key, and the key has to live somewhere the application can reach, typically in the same configuration or secrets store that an attacker who has already breached the application is likely to reach too. The principle to keep is that **a well-designed authentication system should be structurally unable to recover a user's original password**, not 'able but promising not to.' The application's only job is to *verify a claim* ('this login attempt supplies the same password that was originally set'), never to *know* the password.

sections.heading: One-Way Hashing: Verification Without Reversibility
sections.body:
A cryptographic hash function takes an input of any size and deterministically produces a fixed-size output (the *hash* or *digest*), and it is computationally infeasible to work backward from the output to the input. Determinism is what makes verification possible: to check a login attempt, the application hashes the newly entered password and compares that fresh hash with the hash stored at registration. It never tries to decrypt or recover the stored value, because with a proper one-way hash there is no operation that could.

Registration therefore stores `hash(password)`, never `password`, and login re-derives `hash(entered_password)` and compares it with the stored value. If the two match, the entered password was (almost certainly) the string that produced the stored hash, and at no point did the raw password need to be retained beyond the moment it was typed.

sections.heading: Salting: Defeating Precomputed Lookup Tables
sections.body:
A plain, unsalted hash has an exploitable weakness: identical passwords always produce identical hashes. An attacker holding a breached database of hashes doesn't need to attack each one individually. They can precompute hashes for millions of common passwords once (a *rainbow table*) and look up every hash from the breach in it, instantly recovering every user whose password was common, for the cost of building the table once.

A **salt** is random data mixed into the password before hashing to defeat this: `hash(password + salt)` gives a different result for the same password whenever the salt differs, so a table built for one salt is useless against a hash made with another. BCrypt handles salting for you: every call to `encode(rawPassword)` generates a fresh random salt and embeds it in the output string, so you never manage a separate salt column. A BCrypt hash looks like `$2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy`, where `$2a$` identifies the algorithm version, `10` is the cost (work factor, covered next), and the rest encodes the salt and the hash together. That is why `matches(rawPassword, storedHash)` can read the salt back out of the stored hash and re-hash the candidate password with it before comparing.

sections.heading: Deliberately Slow: The Work Factor as a Feature, Not a Bug
sections.body:
General-purpose hash functions like MD5 or plain SHA-256 are *fast*, which makes them good for checksums and data-structure lookups and dangerous for password storage. An attacker with a breached database of fast-hashed passwords can try billions of guesses per second on modern GPU hardware, which makes brute-force and dictionary attacks against the whole leaked database practical, even when the hashes were salted.

BCrypt is deliberately slow, through a configurable **work factor** (also called cost or strength, the `10` in the example hash above) that controls how many rounds of computation each hash performs. The factor is a power of two, so raising it by 1 doubles the time per hash. For one real login the added cost is typically tens of milliseconds, which a user never notices. For an attacker making billions of guesses against a leaked database, the same per-hash cost multiplied across all those attempts is the difference between a brute-force run finishing in hours and one taking centuries. Spring Security's `BCryptPasswordEncoder` defaults to a strength of 10, and its constructor accepts an explicit strength. Current guidance is to *raise* the work factor over time as hardware gets faster, and never to lower it to shave milliseconds off a login endpoint, which would trade away the reason for using BCrypt. Two practical details: BCrypt only uses the first 72 bytes of the input, so older Spring Security versions ignored anything past that, while current ones refuse to encode a longer password (cap the length in your validation); and in a real application you will often build the encoder with `PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder()`, which prefixes each stored hash with its algorithm (`{bcrypt}$2a$10$...`) so that old hashes keep verifying after you move to a stronger scheme.

examples.title: Encoding a Password at Registration
examples.explanation: PasswordEncoder is exposed as an ordinary @Bean, like the beans from the Core Concepts module, so it can be constructor-injected into any service that needs it. encode(rawPassword) generates a fresh random salt and produces a BCrypt hash string with that salt embedded; that string, and only that string, is persisted. The raw password exists only for the duration of this method call and is never written to the database, a log, or anywhere that outlives the request.

examples.title: Verifying a Login Attempt Correctly, and the Wrong Way to Try
examples.explanation: matches(rawPassword, storedHash) exists for this comparison: it reads the salt and work factor embedded in storedHash, re-hashes rawPassword with that same salt and work factor, and only then compares the two hashes, returning true whenever the candidate is right, whatever a fresh hash of the same password would look like. The commented-out WRONG approach calls encode(rawPassword) a second time, which generates a new random salt unrelated to the stored one, so the result differs from the stored hash almost every time, even for the correct password.

examples.title: Two Hashes of the Same Password, Deliberately Different
examples.explanation: hash1 and hash2 come from encoding the same string, "password123", twice, and they look nothing alike, because each call to encode() generates its own random salt and embeds it in the result. hash1.equals(hash2) is false, which is expected and NOT a bug: it follows directly from per-call random salting. Both matches(...) calls return true, because each one extracts the salt embedded in its own stored hash and re-hashes "password123" with that salt before comparing. Verification never depends on two independently produced hashes looking alike.

misconceptions.description: You can verify a login attempt by hashing the entered password yourself with encode(...) and comparing it to the stored hash using .equals() or ==.
misconceptions.clarification: Every call to BCryptPasswordEncoder's encode() generates a new random salt, so hashing the same password twice gives two different strings almost every time. Comparing a freshly encoded hash with a stored one using .equals() fails even when the password is exactly right. The correct approach is passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, storedHash), which extracts the salt embedded in the STORED hash and re-hashes the candidate with it before comparing. That is why matches() takes the raw candidate and the stored hash as separate arguments, instead of comparing two hashes.

misconceptions.description: BCrypt being slow is a performance problem worth working around, for example by lowering its work factor (cost/strength) to make login endpoints respond faster.
misconceptions.clarification: BCrypt's slowness is a deliberate security property, not an inefficiency to optimize away. The extra computation per hash is a few milliseconds a real user never notices, but for an attacker making billions of guesses against a breached database of hashes it is the dominant cost. Lowering the work factor to speed up a login endpoint weakens protection against offline brute-force attacks in direct proportion. The recommended practice is the opposite: raise the work factor periodically as hardware gets faster, so the level of protection doesn't erode.
misconceptions.fact: BCrypt's slowness is a deliberate security property, not an implementation inefficiency to be optimized away.

exercises.prompt: This login method rejects every login attempt as invalid, even when the user enters their password correctly. Find and fix the bug.
hints: encode(...) is called here on every single login attempt -- does BCrypt's encode() produce the exact same output string for the same input every time it's called, or does something change between calls?
Compare this to how the password was originally stored at registration time -- was that stored value produced by this same encode() call, using the same salt?
There's a purpose-built method on PasswordEncoder specifically designed to compare a raw candidate password against an already-stored hash, without needing to generate a matching salt yourself.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The original code calls passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword) on every login attempt, which generates a new random salt each time, unrelated to the salt embedded in the hash stored at registration. Comparing that fresh hash with the stored one using .equals() almost always returns false, because two BCrypt hashes of the same password made with different salts look nothing alike, whether or not the entered password is right. The fix is passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, user.getHashedPassword()), which extracts the salt from the STORED hash, re-hashes the candidate with that salt, and then compares. It is the correct way to verify a password without the raw password ever having been retained.

exercises.prompt: A user's password "correcthorse" was hashed at registration and stored as storedHash. Later, an attacker who has stolen the database tries to brute-force it by calling passwordEncoder.encode("correcthorse") themselves and comparing the result to storedHash using .equals(). Separately, the real login flow calls passwordEncoder.matches("correcthorse", storedHash). Predict the result of each comparison, and explain why they differ despite both starting from the exact correct password.
hints: The attacker's encode("correcthorse") call generates its own brand-new random salt -- is there any reason to expect it would coincidentally match the salt embedded in storedHash from registration?
matches(...) doesn't generate a new salt at all -- it reads whichever salt is already embedded in the storedHash argument you give it.
Both comparisons start from the objectively correct password -- the difference in outcome comes entirely from HOW each one performs its comparison, not from the password being right or wrong.
exercises.expectedAnswer: attackerCheck is (almost certainly) false, because encode("correcthorse") called a second time generates a brand-new, unrelated random salt, producing a hash string that looks nothing like storedHash even though the underlying password is identical. loginCheck is true, because matches(...) extracts the salt already embedded in storedHash itself and re-hashes "correcthorse" using that exact same salt before comparing, which correctly confirms the password matches regardless of what a fresh, independently-salted encode() call would produce.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The attacker's shortcut misunderstands what BCrypt guarantees. encode("correcthorse") does not produce a stable fingerprint of the string; it produces a hash tied to whatever random salt is generated on that call, so two calls with the same input give two different-looking strings almost every time. Comparing the attacker's fresh hash with storedHash using .equals() compares hashes built from two unrelated salts, so it fails whether or not the password is right. A real attacker would instead take the salt embedded in the stolen hash and re-hash each guess with it, which is what matches() does, and that is why the per-hash cost of a high work factor matters. The real login flow uses matches(rawPassword, storedHash), which reads the salt embedded in storedHash (the hash format exists to make this possible) and re-hashes the candidate with it. That is why PasswordEncoder exposes matches() as a separate method, rather than expecting callers to compare two encode() outputs.

assessments.prompt: Calling passwordEncoder.encode("hunter2") twice, back to back, produces two completely different-looking output strings. What is the most accurate explanation, and is this a bug?
options: It's a bug -- a correctly implemented password encoder should produce the identical hash for the identical input every time.
It indicates the PasswordEncoder bean was misconfigured with an inconsistent work factor between the two calls.
It's expected, intended behavior -- each call generates a fresh, random salt that gets embedded in the output.
It's expected, but only because "hunter2" is a well-known example password that BCrypt specifically randomizes further as an extra precaution.
assessments.explanation: BCrypt generates a new random salt on every encode() call and embeds it in the returned hash string. That is intended behavior, not a bug, and it is what defeats precomputed rainbow-table attacks: an attacker can't precompute one hash per common password, because the salt varies each time a hash is produced. The “It's a bug -- a correctly implemented…” option is wrong because the 'correct' behavior it describes is the unsafe, unsalted behavior real password hashing avoids. The “It's expected, but only because "hunter2"…” option is wrong because no password string is special-cased; every input is salted the same way. The “It indicates the PasswordEncoder bean was misconfigured…” option is wrong because any correctly configured BCryptPasswordEncoder behaves this way, at any consistent work factor.

assessments.prompt: A team considers using reversible encryption, with a decryption key stored in the application's own configuration, instead of a one-way hash for storing passwords -- reasoning that at least the database itself won't contain plain text. What is the flaw in this reasoning?
options: Reversible encryption is only insecure if the decryption key happens to be stored in the exact same database table as the encrypted passwords.

The decryption key has to be reachable by the application somewhere, and an attacker who has already breached the application enough to steal the encrypted passwords is very likely to also be able to reach that same key -- at which point every password becomes recoverable in one additional step, which shifts the problem rather than solving it.
There is no real flaw -- reversible encryption is strictly safer than any one-way hash, since it also allows recovering a password for support purposes.
Reversible encryption is mathematically impossible to implement correctly, so an application built this way would simply fail to run.
assessments.explanation: Reversible encryption only shifts the problem: the key that makes decryption possible has to live somewhere the application can reach, typically alongside the configuration or secrets an attacker who has breached the application is likely to reach too. The “There is no real flaw -- reversible…” option treats recoverability as a pure benefit, when it is the property that turns a breach into a catastrophe. The “Reversible encryption is mathematically impossible to implement…” option is false: reversible encryption is easy to implement, and the problem is architectural. The “Reversible encryption is only insecure…” option narrows the risk to one storage mistake, when wherever the key lives, an attacker who can reach the encrypted data has a real chance of reaching the key.

assessments.prompt: A BCrypt hash string looks like `$2a$10$N9qo8uLOickgx2ZMRZoMyeIjZAgcfl7p92ldGxad68LJZdL17lhWy`, and BCrypt does not store a separate salt column anywhere. Given this, what does matches(rawPassword, storedHash) actually do to verify a password?
options: It sends storedHash to a remote key-management service to have it decrypted before comparing against rawPassword.

It ignores the string's internal structure entirely and simply calls encode(rawPassword) again, comparing the two resulting strings directly, which works because encoding the same password always produces the same string as before.
It strips the $2a$10$ prefix and treats the remainder as the plain, unhashed original password for a direct string comparison.

It parses the salt (and work factor) already embedded directly within storedHash itself, re-hashes rawPassword using that exact same extracted salt, and compares the newly computed hash against the stored one.
assessments.explanation: The salt and work factor are encoded in the hash string alongside the hash itself, which lets matches() extract the original salt from the stored hash and re-hash the candidate password with it. No separate salt column is needed. The “It ignores the string's internal structure entirely…” option describes the broken approach from the examples, which fails because encode() uses a fresh random salt on each call. The “It sends storedHash to a remote key-management…” option invents an external decryption step: BCrypt hashes are never decrypted, only recomputed and compared. The “It strips the $2a$10$ prefix and treats…” option misreads the hash string as containing the plain password, which a one-way hash prevents by design.

assessments.prompt: Why does increasing BCrypt's work factor meaningfully hinder an attacker attempting to brute-force a stolen password database, while barely affecting a genuine user logging in?
options: A genuine user performs exactly one hash computation per login attempt, so a few extra milliseconds is imperceptible; an attacker performs that same per-hash cost across billions of guesses, so the same per-hash increase multiplies into a massive difference in total attack time.
The work factor changes the length of the resulting hash string, which slows down brute-force comparisons specifically on hardware with limited memory.
Increasing the work factor causes BCrypt to reject any password attempt shorter than a certain length, filtering out most automated attacks.
The work factor only applies to failed login attempts, so a genuine user who enters the correct password never pays the added computational cost at all.
assessments.explanation: The asymmetry comes from volume. One genuine login pays the per-hash cost once, so even a deliberately slow hash costs that user a few imperceptible milliseconds. An attacker making billions of guesses against a leaked hash database pays the same per-hash cost billions of times, which turns a small fixed increase per hash into an enormous difference in total attack time. The “The work factor only applies to failed…” option is false: the work factor applies to every hash computation, because BCrypt can't know in advance which guess will succeed. The “The work factor changes the length…” option is wrong because the work factor controls computational rounds, not string length. The “Increasing the work factor causes BCrypt…” option invents a length-based rejection rule that BCrypt doesn't have.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer suggests storing passwords with a reversible encryption scheme instead of BCrypt, reasoning that 'if we ever need to recover a user's password for support purposes, we can just decrypt it.' Explain why this reasoning is flawed, and explain how BCrypt's salting and deliberate slowness address the real underlying risks that plain or reversible storage doesn't.
assessments.modelAnswer: The junior developer treats 'being able to recover the original password' as a feature, but for password storage that capability is the core risk. A well-designed authentication system doesn't need to know a user's password after the moment it was set. Its only job afterward is to verify a CLAIM ('this login attempt supplies the same password as before'), and that can be done without being able to reconstruct the original string. Reversible encryption keeps reconstruction possible by definition, so the decryption key has to be available to the application, and whoever compromises the application (likely the same attacker who already breached the database) is very likely to reach the key too, at which point every stored password is recoverable in one step. That is plain-text storage with one extra step added for the attacker. A one-way hash like BCrypt avoids the problem because it is computationally infeasible to reverse: there is no key that could 'decrypt' a BCrypt hash, because the operation only goes one way. Verification re-hashes the login attempt and compares it with the stored hash, with no reversal. BCrypt adds two protections that plain hashing lacks. It generates and embeds a random salt in every hash, so even two users with the identical password get different stored hashes, which defeats precomputed lookup tables across a breached database. And it makes each hash deliberately slow through a tunable work factor, which costs a genuine user a few milliseconds per login but multiplies into an enormous amount of compute for an attacker making billions of guesses against a stolen database. Together, irreversibility, per-password salting and deliberate slowness address the three realistic threats to a breached password store (recovery, precomputed lookup and brute force) in a way plain text or reversible encryption cannot, however reasonable 'just in case we need to recover it' sounds.
